The message was brief. “Dr. Waldron, would you call Mrs. Jones back about her labs?”

I was puzzled. I didn’t remember ordering any labs for Mrs. Jones. As far as I could remember, she was seeing a specialist and just had surgery for colon cancer. Maybe they had ordered the labs. But if so, they certainly should have followed up on them.

I opened the chart and looked in the lab section. Quickly my eye went to my patient’s kidney function and stopped. Her kidney function had declined a huge amount in the last week.

I called her and then her kidney specialist. Over the next half hour, her situation came into view. Because of her colon surgery, she was losing a lot of fluid, enough that she couldn’t keep up. This, in turn, was making her kidney function a lot worse, along with dropping her potassium level.

To take care of it, she would need IV fluids – once or twice a week – to keep up with the fluids she was losing. Without that, her kidneys would shut down completely.

In a sense, Mrs. Jones was dealing with kidney burnout—a situation where they were putting out more than they were taking in and suffering as a result.

As I was thinking about this, my mind went to the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is “Dead” because it has such a high level of minerals and salts that very few, other than a few microorganisms, can survive.

The reason for this is that the Dead Sea has no outlet. The Jordan River drains into it, carrying fresh water, and then sits in a basin. Some of the water evaporates, and what remains are the salts and minerals in the water.

Over the thousands of years since the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah, this inland body of water has become one of the saltiest places on earth. It is a body of water that is neither useful for irrigation nor a place where plants and animals can thrive.

Neither situation is healthy, yet this is exactly how most people live their lives, typically gravitating towards one pole or the other. Either they fill their schedule to the maximum, leaving no time for quiet reflection, or they resist any efforts to get them to invest their time and talents and avoid these sorts of activities.

I want to spend a little time thinking about burnout. What causes it, and how we can avoid it?

Everyone has Limits

I Samuel 30 tells the story of David returning to Ziklag. Upon his arrival, he discovered, to his dismay, that the Amalekites had invaded Philistine territory, burned the town, and taken captive all the people who were present.

David and his men had been gone three days and were already tired from their journey to and from Aphek, where King Agag had mustered his forces. Despite this and their anguish at the loss of their family members and material possessions, David consulted God and decided to pursue to the Amalekites out into the desert.

They had only gone as far as the Brook Besor when a third of his men gave up. Scripture tells us they were “too faint” to cross the brook. They were physically and mentally exhausted. Even if they had been able to hold things together for another day, they would be useless in battle.

So it was that David left them behind and continued to pursue the Amalekites, eventually defeating them with the four hundred men who were able to persevere. Here, we come to the interesting part. The men who had won the victory looked down on the men who had been faint. They said those faint-hearted men could have their families back, but all the spoil would be reserved for those who had won the victory.

In response, David said, “Ye shall not do so, my brethren, with that which the Lord hath given us, who hath preserved us, and delivered the company that came against us into our hand. For who will hearken unto you in this matter? but as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike.” (I Samuel 30:23,24)

David did not wish to penalize those who had tried but did not have the strength to make it through to the final battle.

Perhaps this speaks of the grace we ought to extend to others who don’t have the strength or energy to continue for a season. Maybe it lets us know that we should extend that same grace to ourselves.

What is Burnout?

There are different definitions for burnout, but it all comes down to a state of physical, mental, or emotional exhaustion related to too much stress over an extended period of time. We tend to think of this stress as work-related. There are too many projects going on at once, not enough help, or an employer who has high expectations.

Stress is stress, and it all adds up. Even if work isn’t stressful, if you have a newborn baby at home, a family member with dementia, or many church responsibilities, you can still reach the place where you have little left to give.

It is as though you are in a vehicle traveling 90 mph, and you push the accelerator a little harder, and nothing happens. In response, you push the gas pedal even harder, and a screeching noise comes from the engine. Suddenly, the dashboard lights up with funny lights, and the car starts to slow down.

The question is, how can we avoid burnout and what should we do if we realize that we are heading towards it?

Understanding Burnout

Burnout leads to both physical and emotional depletion. The problem with burnout is that even if a particular stressor causes it – say, a situation at work or a family health problem – it will affect numerous other relationships.

People dealing with burnout often exhibit symptoms consistent with depression and anxiety. They may become withdrawn, lack motivation to be involved with church and family activities, or get angry quicker than people who are not dealing with burnout.

There is even a suggestion that burnout can lead to the weakening of our immune systems. This could lead to more colds and viral infections.

Identify Early Signs

We need to know ourselves. There are signs that other people can see in our lives and how we relate to others that we don’t necessarily identify as a problem.

People who are on the edge of burnout feel hopeless. They may hide it from their coworkers, but often, their family members realize that something is wrong. You used to have a sunny disposition, and now you are discouraged, not only about the present but also the future.

You might lack motivation and have low energy levels. In a sense, you are going through the motions and just doing enough to get by – both at work and in your home. This is likely related to your feelings of hopelessness.

You may find that you are more irritable than you used to be. Little things bother or aggravate you, and you find yourself smothering angry retorts.

It is important to realize that you are heading down this road for several reasons. First, you are not the only one who suffers when you are burned out. Your family must deal with you and your “grumpiness.” Also, the longer you go without taking care of things, the harder it is to get back to a place of balance.

As a physician, I see people all the time who “didn’t have time” to get something taken care of until they could no longer ignore it. At this point, it will take a major procedure to set things right. It would have been easier to correct if they came in with the first symptom.

Make a Priority List

Everything in our life has a priority level. People who do not prioritize end up feeling scattered as they try to do everything at once. This is a recipe for disaster. To me, it makes sense to divide our tasks into four buckets:

  1. Things that need to be done relatively quickly
  2. Things that need to be done but can wait a bit
  3. Things that we’d like to do, but don’t need to
  4. Things that we should let go of.

Here might be a good place to mention that just because something needs to be done does not mean you need to do it. Sometimes, someone in your home or workplace could help with one of the tasks on your to-do list.

Once we have made our priority list, we need to do something about it. If you simply assign a priority to everything in your life but continue to try to do everything, it won’t help your situation at all.

The point of this exercise is to figure out what things you can eliminate from your schedule, so you have more space to breathe.

Make First Things First

One of the things that happens when we are overwhelmed is that we stop doing self-care. We grab unhealthy food on the go, stop spending time in prayer and devotions, and quit exercising.

Doing these things takes time, and that is exactly what we think we don’t have when we are living on the margins of our energy. Self-care is extremely important but often gets assigned a priority of zero and is seldom included in a day’s activity.

As we begin to replenish our spiritual nourishment, we must also make sure we take care of our physical health.

Take Time Apart

After feeding the multitudes, Mark 6:46 tells of Jesus, “And when he had sent them away, he departed into a mountain to pray.” Even Jesus had times when He needed to be alone without distractions.

It is easy to focus on the prayer aspect of this passage, and that is important, but let's focus on the solitary aspect of this experience. Jesus even left His closest followers behind during this time of seeking God’s face.

There are times when we need to escape from the pressure of human interactions and find a peaceful place where we can be alone.

Put Down Technology

Part of making rest time truly restful is to eliminate sources of distraction. Phones and electronic tablets are exactly the types of things that can keep our minds from achieving the peace (shalom) that we both desire and need.

Digital burnout is a new term that is being used to describe people who feel apathetic and exhausted from spending hours each day staring at screens. Many workers spend seven or eight hours a day looking at computer screens and then get even more screen time after work.

The funny thing is that the most productive workers are often people who use old-fashioned things like paper calendars and leave phones out of meetings. As wonderful as phones are, they are also immensely distracting for most of us.

So often, we have time away that is simply not restful. The reason is that we continue to receive texts and emails and can still access social media. If you are not someone who can put his phone away and ignore it (it takes a lot of willpower to do this), then leave your phone in another room and create some distance. This will seem stressful, but we can focus on recharging ourselves by creating a screen-free zone.

Build Breaks into Your Day

There is a certain amount of work that must be done each day, and it often feels like too much for the allotted 24 hours. There is certainly no time to stop, stretch, and take a five-minute walk, or at least that's what we tell ourselves.

In reality, if you take a five-minute break every few hours to do something non-work related, you will come back refreshed and more ready to deal with the problems of the day.

Do something healthy during this time. Take a short walk or eat an apple. Chowing down a bag of potato chips or eating a couple candy bars is not likely to produce the desired results.

The problem is often with our own expectations. People who struggle with burnout often have extremely high personal standards and get frustrated when they not measure up to that standard.

Be Intentional about Rest

One of the messages of the Old Testament was the importance of the Sabbath. I have heard many people argue that in the New Testament period, we no longer need to practice the Sabbath. Didn’t Paul say that one day was like the other? Didn’t Jesus defend His disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath?

Regardless of what you believe about the importance of keeping the Sabbath, it is still important that we take time to rest. This is the real message that Jesus was conveying when He said that the “Sabbath was created for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Rest is not simply sleeping till 10 am and then doing nothing. Rest is actively making decisions that will help us recharge our depleted batteries. Go out for breakfast with a friend, take a hike, or take a good book and go somewhere without cell service and focus on something other than situations that are depleting you.

Jesus understood the human need for rest, this is why He told His disciples “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). This time of rest would give them energy for their next time of ministry.

Don’t Buy into Myths

People tell themselves all sorts of lies that can lead to pushing themselves too hard. I’ll list a few of them and some thoughts about each one.

“I’m the only one who can do this task.” This feels true. The other people in our home or workplace are not helping us the way we wish that they would. Sometimes, it simply feels easier to do the task ourselves rather than spend time teaching someone else how to do it. We need to remember that if we died, the people around us would figure out how to get things done. We can assign them some of the tasks today before we die.

“If I just get this job done today, tomorrow will be easier.” I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but each day has 24 hours, and somehow, they always get filled up. I have given up the idea that there is a time in my life coming up soon that will have nothing on the schedule. If a rest comes, it will come because I have made an effort to clear my schedule, not because by some random occurrence, one day, I happen to not have a single task in it.

“God will never give me more than I can handle.” God has promised many things. He has promised that when there is a temptation, He will give us an opportunity to escape it (I Corinthians 10:13). He has also promised that He will never leave us or forsake us (Hebrews 13:5). I do not read anywhere in Scripture that God will keep us from overfilling our lives. He has simply promised that He will give us opportunity to take a different path and will walk beside us on our way.

So often the heavy load we carry is because other people, or even we, ourselves, have put too many things on our task list. Suppose I choose to put too many patients on my schedule and I am feeling exhausted. In that case, it is time for me to take responsibility for what I have done, rather than claiming a mythical promise that God will keep me from overwhelming myself.

“These are all good things that I am doing.” Doctors face this a lot. We want to squeeze one more patient into the schedule and stay just a little later to answer another message because we feel responsible. We hate to think that someone might need to go to the Emergency Department because we did not take care of them when they needed help.

Just because the things in your schedule are “good things” that benefit other people and are building the kingdom, does not mean that you don’t need to cut back in one area or another. If you are feeling emotionally depleted, it is probably time to remove a few items from your to-do list.

Conclusion

There are other things that could be mentioned. Getting support from someone else, meditating on Scripture, and even taking a vacation are all things that can help.

When I read about some of the famous preachers of the past, I see in some of their lives a roller coaster. They pushed themselves to the max, got involved in large numbers of projects, and then had an emotional breakdown. They would take some time off and, a month or two later, launch back into the same activities. This cycle continued for their whole ministry.

Jesus tells us that His yoke is easy, and His burden is light (Matt, 11:28-30). If we are at the point of exhaustion, we need to consider whether we have Jesus’ yoke or if we are laboring under the burden of our own creation.

Jesus knows our limitations. He wants us to have balance, living in such a way that we not only have strength for today but also for tomorrow, next week, and next year – till He comes again.

Somo lilikuwa fupi. “Dkt. Waldron, unaweza kumpigia Mrs. Jones kurudi kuhusu matokeo yake ya maabara?”

Nilikasirika. Sikumbuki kuagiza maabara yoyote kwa Mrs. Jones. Kadri nilivyokumbuka, alikuwa akimtazama mtaalam na alikuwa amepewa upasuaji kwa saratani ya kolon tu. Labda wao walikuwa wameagiza maabara. Lakini ikiwa ni hivyo, kwa hakika wangepaswa kufuatilia matokeo hayo.

Nilifungua rekodi na kutazama sehemu ya maabara. Ghafla macho yangu yalielekezwa kwa kazi ya figo ya mgonjwa wangu na yakasimama. Kazi yake ya figo ilikuwa imeshuka kwa kiasi kikubwa katika wiki iliyopita.

Nimempigia yeye halafu daktari wa figo. Katika nusu saa iliyofuata, hali yake ilianza kuwa wazi. Kwa sababu ya upasuaji wa kolon, alikuwa akipoteza kiasi kikubwa cha maji mwilini, vya kutosha kwamba hakuweza kuyafuatilia. Hii, kwa upande mwingine, ilikuwa ikifanya kazi ya figo yake kuwa mbaya zaidi, pamoja na kushuka kwa kiwango chake cha potasiamu.

Ili kutatuliwa, angehitaji maji ya kuingizwa kwa vena (IV) — mara moja au mbili kwa wiki — ili kufidia maji anayopoteza. Bila hayo, figo zake zingefunga kabisa.

Kwa namna fulani, Mrs. Jones alikuwa akikabiliwa na uchovu wa figo — hali ambapo zinatoa zaidi ya zinavyopokelewa na kuumia kwa matokeo.

Nilipokuwa nikifikiria hili, akili yangu ilielekea Bahari ya Wafu. Bahari ya Wafu ni “Wafu” kwa sababu ina kiwango cha juu sana cha madini na chumvi kiasi kwamba wachache tu, isipokuwa baadhi ya viumbe vidogo, wanaweza kuishi.

Sababu ya hili ni kwamba Bahari ya Wafu haina njia ya kutiririka. Mto Yordani unaingia ndani yake, ukileta maji safi, kisha ukalala kwenye bakuli. Sehemu ya maji huvukiza, na kile kinachobaki ni chumvi na madini yaliyomo ndani ya maji.

Kutokana na maelfu ya miaka tangu kuanguka kwa Sodoma na Gomora, mwili huu wa maji wa ndani umekuwa mojawapo ya maeneo yenye chumvi nyingi duniani. Ni mwili wa maji usiofaa kwa umwagiliaji wala mahali ambapo mimea na wanyama wanaweza kustawi.

Hakuna mojawapo ya hali hizi za afya, lakini hivi ndivyo watu wengi huishi maisha yao, mara nyingi wakielekea upande mmoja au mwingine. Wao wanaweza kujaza ratiba yao hadi kiwango cha juu kabisa, bila nafasi ya tafakari kimya, au wanakataa jitihada zozote za kuwafanya waweke wakati na vipaji vyao na kuepuka aina hizi za shughuli.

Nataka kutumia muda kidogo kufikiri kuhusu uchovu wa kazi. Nini husababisha, na tunavyoweza kuepuka?

Kila Mtu Ana Mipaka

1 Samweli 30 inasimulia hadithi ya Daudi akiendelea kurudi Ziklag. Alipowasili, aligundua, kwa kuhuzunika kwake, kwamba Waamaleki walivamia eneo la Wafilisti, waliteketeza mji, na kuwachukua mateka watu wote waliokuwepo.

Daudi na wanamume wake walikuwa wameondoka kwa siku tatu na tayari walikuwa wamechoka kutokana na safari yao ya kwenda na kurudi kutoka Apheki, ambapo Mfalme Agagi alikuwa amekusanya jeshi lake. Licha ya hili na uchungu wao kwa kupoteza wapendwa wao na mali, Daudi aliomba kushauriana na Mungu na akamua kuwafuata Waamaleki hadi jangwani.

Walikuwa wameenda hadi Mto Besori tu wakati theluthi mmoja ya wanamume wake walikata tamaa. Maandiko yanatuambia walikuwa “wapuuzaji” kupita kiasi kutavuka mto. Walikuwa wamechoka kimwili na kiakili. Hata kama wangeweza kusimamia siku nyingine, wangekuwa havina maana katika vita.

Hivyo Daudi aliwaacha nyuma na kuendelea kuwafuata Waamaleki, hatimaye kuwashinda kwa wanamume mia nne ambao waliweza kustahimili. Hapa tunakuja sehemu ya kuvutia. Wanamume waliopata ushindi waliwaangalia wale waliokuwa wamelala moyo. Walisema wanaume wale waoga waweze kurudishiwa familia zao, lakini washindi wangehifadhiwa kila kitu cha mafao.

Daudi akajibu, “Hamfanyi hivyo, ndugu zangu, kwa yale ambayo Bwana ametupatia, amewatunza na akatuokoa; nami ameweka wapinzani walioingia kwetu mikononi mwetu. Kwa maana nani atakaye sikiliza kwenu katika jambo hili? Bali kama sehemu yake ya yule anayeenda kupigana, ndivyo pia sehemu yake ya yule anayesimama karibu na bidhaa: wote watagawana pamoja.” (1 Samweli 30:23,24)

Daudi hakutaka kuadhibu wale ambao walijaribu lakini hawakuwa na nguvu za kufika hadi mapigano ya mwisho.

Labda hili linaonyesha neema tunayopaswa kuwapa wengine ambao hawana nguvu au nishati ya kuendelea kwa msimu fulani. Labda pia linatufahamisha kwamba tunapaswa kuelekeza neema hiyo kwa sisi wenyewe.

Uchovu wa Kazi Ni Nini?

Kuna ufafanuzi tofauti kwa uchovu wa kazi, lakini yote yanarejea kwenye hali ya uchovu wa kimwili, kisaikolojia, au kihisia unaohusishwa na msongo wa mawazo wa muda mrefu. Tunahisi mara nyingi msongo huu uko kuhusiana na kazi. Kuna miradi mingi kwa wakati mmoja, msaada mdogo, au mwajiri mwenye matarajio makubwa.

Msongo ni msongo, na yote hujikusanya. Hata kama kazi siyo chanzo cha msongo, ikiwa una mtoto mchanga nyumbani, mwanachama wa familia mwenye ugonjwa wa kumbukumbu, au wajibu mwingi wa kanisani, bado unaweza kufika mahali ambapo huna kitu cha kutoa.

Kama vile uko katika gari unaosafiri kwa maili 90 kwa saa, unabana mguu wa gesi kidogo zaidi, na hakuna kinachotokea. Kwa kujibu, unabana gesi kwa nguvu zaidi, na sauti ya kusurika inatoka kwenye injini. Ghafla, dashibodi inajaa taa za ajabu, na gari inaanza kupunguza mwendo.

Swali ni, tunaweza kuiepuka vipi uchovu wa kazi na tunapaswa kufanya nini tukigundua tunazidi kuuelekea?

Kuelewa Uchovu wa Kazi

Uchovu wa kazi husababisha upungufu wa kimwili na kihisia. Tatizo la uchovu wa kazi ni kwamba hata kama chanzo fulani cha msongo ndicho kimesababisha — sema, hali kazini au shida ya afya ya familia — itatafika kwa mahusiano mengine mengi.

Watu wanaokumbwa na uchovu wa kazi mara nyingi huonyesha dalili zinazofanana na unyogovu na wasiwasi. Wanaweza kujiondoa, kukosa motisha ya kushiriki katika shughuli za kanisa na familia, au kuchukizwa haraka zaidi kuliko watu wasiokumbwa na uchovu huo.

Kuna hata mapendekezo kwamba uchovu wa kazi unaweza kusababisha udhaifu wa mfumo wetu wa kinga. Hii inaweza kupelekea mafua na maambukizi ya virusi mara kwa mara.

Tambua Dalili za Mapema

Tunahitaji kujijua. Kuna dalili ambazo watu wengine wanaweza kuziwona katika maisha yetu na jinsi tunavyohusiana na wengine ambazo hatutambulii kuwa tatizo.

Watu walio karibu na kuingia kwenye uchovu wa kazi wanahisi kukata tamaa. Wanaweza kuficha hili kwa wenzake wa kazi, lakini mara nyingi, familia yao hugundua kwamba kuna kitu kibaya. Ulikuwa na tabasamu mara nyingi, na sasa umechoshwa, siyo tu kuhusu sasa bali pia kuhusu siku za usoni.

Unaweza kukosa motisha na kuwa na kiwango cha chini cha nishati. Kwa namna fulani, unafanya tu mambo kwa mtiririko wa kawaida ukifanya vya kutosha tu kuvuka — kazini na nyumbani. Hii inaweza kuhusiana na hisia zako za kukata tamaa.

Unaweza kubaini kuwa wewe ni mtu mwenye hasira zaidi kuliko kawaida. Mambo madogo yanakukera au kunyanyasa, na unajikuta ukitulia majibu ya hasira.

Ni muhimu kutambua kwamba unaelekea njia hii kwa sababu kadhaa. Kwanza, si wewe peke yako anayeteseka unapotokana na uchovu. Familia yako lazima iwashughulikie wewe na “ukakasi” wako. Pia, kadri unavyokwenda bila kutatua mambo, ndivyo inavyokuwa vigumu zaidi kupata usawa tena.

Kama daktari, ninaona watu kila mara ambao “hawakuwa na muda” wa kushughulikia jambo mpaka wakiwa hawawezi tena kuizuia. Wakati huo, itahitaji taratibu kuu kurekebisha. Ingeninga kwa urahisi zaidi iwapo wangekuja wakiwa na dalili ya kwanza.

Fanya Orodha ya Kipaumbele

Kila kitu katika maisha yetu kina kiwango cha kipaumbele. Watu wasioweka vipaumbele wanajikuta wamegawanyika wanapojaribu kufanya kila kitu kwa wakati mmoja. Hii ni kichocheo cha maafa. Kwangu, inaonekana busara kugawa majukumu yetu katika makapu manne:

  1. Mambo yanayohitajika kufanywa haraka
  2. Mambo yanayohitajika kufanywa lakini yanaweza kusubiri kidogo
  3. Mambo tunayopenda kufanya, lakini hayahitajiki
  4. Mambo ambayo tunapaswa kuyaacha.

Hapa ni mahali pazuri kutaja kwamba kwa sababu kitu kinahitaji kufanywa haimaanishi lazima ufanye wewe mwenyewe. Wakati mwingine, mtu nyumbani kwako au kazini anaweza kusaidia na moja ya kazi kwenye orodha yako.

Mara tu tukifanya orodha ya vipaumbele, tunahitaji kuchukua hatua. Ikiwa utaweka tu kipaumbele kwa kila kitu katika maisha yako lakini ukaendelea kujaribu kufanya kila kitu, haitasaidia kabisa.

Madhumuni ya zoezi hili ni kubaini mambo unayoweza kuondoa kwenye ratiba yako, ili upate nafasi zaidi ya kupumua.

Weka Kwanza Mambo Muhimu

Kimoja kati ya mambo yanayotokea tunapofadhaika ni kwamba tunaacha kujitunza. Tunachukua chakula kisicho na afya tunapotembea, tunaacha kutumia muda katika sala na maombi, na kuacha mazoezi.

Kufanya mambo haya kunachukua muda, na hiyo ndiyo hasa tunafikiria hatuna wakati tunapoishi kwa kikomo cha nishati yetu. Kujitunza ni muhimu sana lakini mara nyingi kunapewa kipaumbele cha sifuri na kidogo huingizwa kwenye shughuli za siku.

Tunapoanza kujaza upya lishe yetu ya kiroho, lazima pia tuhakikishe tunajali afya yetu ya mwili.

Chukua Muda Peke Yako

Baada ya kumlisha umati, Marko 6:46 inasema kuhusu Yesu, “Na baada ya kuwa wamemwacha, yeye peke yake alikwenda juu ya mlima kulilia.” Hata Yesu alikuwa na wakati ambapo alihitaji kuwa peke yake bila usumbufu.

Ni rahisi kuzingatia kipengele cha sala katika aya hii, na hilo ni muhimu, lakini tuzingatie kipengele cha kuwa peke ya mtu katika uzoefu huu. Yesu hata alimuacha waabudu wake wa karibu nyuma wakati wa kipindi hiki cha kutafuta uso wa Mungu.

Kuna nyakati ambazo tunahitaji kutoroka kutoka kwa shinikizo la mwingiliano wa binadamu na kupata mahali pa amani ambapo tunaweza kuwa peke yetu.

Weka Teknolojia Pembeni

Sehemu ya kufanya muda wa mapumziko uwe wa kweli ni kuondoa vyanzo vya usumbufu. Simu na vidonge vya elektroniki ni aina za vitu vinavyoweza kuzuia akili yetu kufikia amani (shalom) tunayotaka na tunayohitaji.

Uchovu wa kidijitali ni neno jipya linalotumika kuelezea watu wanaohisi kupoteza hamu na kuchoka kutokana na kutazama skrini kwa masaa kila siku. Wafanyakazi wengi hutumia saa saba au nane kwa siku kutazama skrini za kompyuta na kisha kuendelea tena baada ya kazi.

Kitu cha kuchekesha ni kwamba wafanyakazi wenye tija mara nyingi ni wale wanaotumia vitu vya zamani kama kalenda za karatasi na kuacha simu nje ya mikutano. Ingawa simu ni nzuri, pia ni vichocheo vikubwa kwa wengi wetu.

Mara nyingi, tunakuwa na muda wa mbali ambao si wa kupumzika kabisa. Sababu ni kwamba tunaendelea kupokea maandishi na barua pepe na bado tunafikika mitandao ya kijamii. Ikiwa wewe si mtu anayeeza kuweka simu yake mbali na kuisiacha (inahitaji nguvu ya ndani kubwa kufanya hivyo), basi wacha simu yako katika chumba kingine na tengeneza umbali. Hii itaonekana kuwa na msongo, lakini tunaweza kujikita katika kujajaza nguvu kwa kuunda eneo lisilo na skrini.

Jenga Mapumziko Kwenye Siku Yako

Kuna kazi fulani inayopaswa kufanywa kila siku, na mara nyingi inahisi ni nyingi mno kwa masaa 24 yaliyotengwa. Hakika hakuna wakati wa kusimama, kunyoosha, na kutembea kwa dakika tano, au angalau ndivyo tunavyojisemea.

Katika ukweli, ikiwa utachukua mapumziko ya dakika tano kila baada ya masaa machache kufanya kitu kisichohusiana na kazi, utafika umechoka kidogo na kuwa tayari zaidi kukabiliana na matatizo ya siku.

Fanya kitu cha kiafya wakati huu. Tembea kwa dakika fupi au kula tufaha. Kula chipsi za viazi au micro ya sukari siyo matokeo yanayotarajiwa.

Tatizo mara nyingi liko katika matarajio yetu wenyewe. Watu wanaopambana na uchovu wa kazi mara nyingi wana viwango vya juu sana vya matarajio binafsi na huzunguka wanaposhindwa kufikia kiwango hicho.

Kuwa Makusudi Kuhusu Kupumzika

Moja ya ujumbe wa Agano la Kale ulikuwa umuhimu wa Sabato. Nimesikia watu wengi wakidai kwamba katika Agano Jipya hatuhitaji tena kuadhimisha Sabato. Je, Paulo hakusema kwamba siku moja ni kama nyingine? Je, Yesu hakamtetea mwanafunzi wake alipochuma nafaka siku ya Sabato?

Bila kujali unaamini nini kuhusu umuhimu wa kuifanya Sabato, bado ni muhimu kuchukua muda wa kupumzika. Huu ndiyo ujumbe halisi ambao Yesu alikuwa akutoa aliposema kwamba “Sabato umetengenezwa kwa ajili ya mwanadamu, si mwanadamu kwa ajili ya Sabato” (Marko 2:27).

Kupumzika si tu kulala hadi saa 10 asubuhi kisha kutofanya chochote. Kupumzika ni kufanya maamuzi kwa makusudi yatakayosaidia kujaza upya betri zetu zilizochoka. Nenda kula kifungua kinywa na rafiki, fanya matembezi, au chukua kitabu kizuri na uende mahali pasipo huduma ya simu na ujielekeze kwenye kitu mbali na hali zinazokuchosha.

Yesu alielewa haja ya mwanadamu ya kupumzika, ndiyo sababu akamwambia wanafunzi wake “Nanyi tujiondoe kidogo kwa mahali penye upweke, mkapumzike” (Marko 6:31). Muda huu wa kupumzika ungewapa nishati kwa utumishi wao uliokuja.

Usikubali Hadithi Potofu

Watu hujiambia hadithi mbalimbali ambazo zinaweza kuwasukuma wajisukume kupita kiasi. Nitataja chache na mawazo kuhusu kila moja.

“Mimi ndiye tu anayefanya kazi hii.” Hii inaonekana kweli. Wengine nyumbani kwetu au kazini hawatusaidii kama tunavyotaka. Wakati mwingine, ni rahisi zaidi kufanya kazi mwenyewe kuliko kutumia muda kumfundisha mwingine jinsi ya kuitenda. Tunapaswa kukumbuka kwamba tukifa, watu waliotuzunguka wangepata njia ya kufanya mambo. Tunaweza kuwapa baadhi ya wajibu leo kabla hatujafariki.

“Ikiwa nitamaliza kazi hii leo, kesho itakuwa rahisi.” Napenda kuleta habari mbaya, lakini kila siku ina masaa 24, na kwa namna fulani, daima hujazana. Nimeacha wazo kwamba kuna siku fulani maisha yangu yatakuwa bila kitu chochote kwenye ratiba. Ikiwa mapumziko yatakuwepo, yatafika kwa sababu nimefanya juhudi ya kuondoa ratiba, si kwa bahati kwamba siku moja sitakuwa na kazi yoyote.

“Mungu hatatanipa zaidi ya niwezayo kubeba.” Mungu ameahidi mambo mengi. Ameahidi kwamba wakati wa jaribio, Atatupatia njia ya kukwepa (1 Wakorintho 10:13). Pia ameahidi kwamba hatatutuacha wala kutuachia (Waebrania 13:5). Mhandisi siwezi kusoma mahali popote katika Maandiko kwamba Mungu atatuzuia kujajaza maisha yetu kupita kiasi. Ameahidi tu kwamba atatupa fursa ya kuchagua njia nyingine na atatembea pamoja nasi tunapopita.

Mara nyingi mzigo mzito tunaobeba ni kwa sababu watu wengine, au hata sisi wenyewe, tumeweka vitu vingi mno kwenye orodha ya majukumu. Ikiwa ninabeba wagonjwa wengi mno kwenye ratiba yangu na nahisi kuchoka, ni wakati wa kuchukua uwajibikaji kwa kile nilichokifanya, badala ya kudai hadithi potofu kwamba Mungu atakunizuia kujazaa maisha yangu kupita kiasi.

“Haya yote ni mambo mema ninayofanya.” Madaktari wanakutana na hili mara nyingi. Tunataka kuongeza mgonjwa mmoja tu kwenye ratiba na kukaa kidogo jioni kujibu ujumbe mwingine kwa sababu tunajisikia kuwajibika. Tunahofu kufikiria kwamba mtu angehitaji kwenda Idara ya Dharura kwa sababu hatukuwa tayari kumsaidia alipohitaji.

Kwa sababu vitu kwenye ratiba yako ni “mambo mema” yanayomsaidia mtu mwingine na kujenga ufalme, haimaanishi kwamba huna haja ya kupunguza katika eneo fulani. Ikiwa unahisi umechoka kihisia, ni wakati wa kuondoa vitu vichache kwenye orodha yako ya kufanya.

Hitimisho

Kuna mambo mengine ambayo yanaweza kutajwa. Kupata msaada kutoka kwa mtu mwingine, kutafakari Maandiko, na hata kwenda mapumziko ni mambo yote ambayo yanaweza kusaidia.

Ninaposoma kuhusu baadhi ya wachungaji mashuhuri wa zamani, ninaona katika baadhi ya maisha yao mzunguko wa mwinuko na kushuka. Walijisukuma hadi kiwango cha juu, wakajihusisha katika miradi mingi, kisha wakapata mshtuko wa kihisia. Wangepumzika kwa muda, na mwezi au miwili baadaye, kuanza tena shughuli zile zile. Mzunguko huu uliendelea katika huduma yao yote.

Yesu anatueleza kwamba mzigo Wake ni mwepesi, na mzigo Wake ni mwepesi (Mathayo 11:28-30). Ikiwa tuko mahali pa uchovu, tunapaswa kuzingatia kama tunabeba yoke ya Yesu au tukibeba mzigo tuliojiwekea wenyewe.

Yesu anafahamu mipaka yetu. Anatamani tuwe na usawa, kuishi kwa njia ambayo si tu tunapata nguvu kwa leo bali pia kesho, wiki ijayo, na mwaka ujao — mpaka atakaporudi tena.

I doubt that there is a soul alive that has not been offended at one time or another. The persistent weeds of evil influence seem to sprout at every corner, testing the best of blooming relationships. The more communication tools we possess, the more miscommunication we seem to encounter, and people are offended. Ministers of the Gospel today are expected to be soft and effeminate lest they offend their listeners. While we certainly must meet people where they are and seek not to offend them, the bane of the modern church is not the bold and offensive minister.

I wish to give no license to hardhearted preachers who are void of tenderness and tears. Woe be unto the dry-eyed prophets who wield the sword of the Lord without an ounce of consideration that there are real people between the ears that they are chopping off in the process. Yet, it seems that there is an epidemic of our day that has surpassed the bubonic plague, outstripped the damage of polio, and makes our modern cancer appear like a minor inconvenience. I speak to the outbreak of the millions of offended hearts that are arising from the rubbish of the innumerable hordes of broken and strained relationships about us on every hand. Jesus mentioned that one of the signs of the end times is that “then shall many be offended . . . and shall hate one another” (Matthew 24:10). Divorce-riddled homes have risen to an all-time high, producing a generation of immense mistrust and pain. Couples will deem themselves as incompatible and separate at the slightest offense. Christians will spend years outside a church setting because they have been offended by fellow believers.

Many will automatically side with the offended party, assuming them to be a victim. Many times they are. “Woe unto the world because of offences!” (Matthew 18:7) But the equation changes when we consider that the sinless Christ offended many. He told His disciples that they must eat His flesh and many left Him. He informed the inner 12 that had stuck with Him, “All ye shall be offended because of me this night” (Mark 14:27). The Pharisees were offended when Christ exposed their vain worship, and Jesus offended His own countrymen simply by doing good. The Greek word is skandalízō meaning “to scandalize”.1 In Hebrew, it means “a stumbling block”. The problem is that many today will stumble over the slightest obstruction in their path and the molehill becomes a mountain.

“Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them” (Psalm 119:165). What shall we say then to this passage? Here are people who have learned how to walk upon the rocky path of life without going down every time a discomfiting obstacle arises before them. We wish to heap no condemnation upon the sensitive soul, but the word sensitive is not in the Bible. The closest word we can find there is sensual, which is very similar in its roots and means natural. Christ described these plants as having “not root in himself, but dureth for a while: for when tribulation or persecution ariseth because of the word, by and by he is offended” (Matthew 13:20-21). It is so easy and very natural to feel sorry for the offended. They carry a tremendous sob story, and they usually share it in tears. “In many things, we offend all” (James 3:2). No one is as sinless in their offending as Christ, so there is usually an element of truth poured out against the offender. It seems to me that we all would be much further down the road if we would withhold some of our sympathy for the offended and spend our energies teaching them how to walk upright on the path of life despite the jagged and copious stumbling stones that greet us daily upon our journey. We will learn to live life unoffended when we learn to . . .

Walk Worthy

“I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called, with all lowliness and meekness, with longsuffering, forbearing one another in love” (Ephesians 4:1-2). To walk worthy, as Paul describes it here, is to walk in humility. “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). The more pride-laden our vessel, the more apt we are to be offended. The more honestly we appraise our worth, the less offended we shall be when derided. More humble equals less stumble. When we are accused of a wrong, it always hurts. Jesus says that we should be happy when people say all manner of evil against us falsely. While such a demeaning wound may fester under our skin, there is a condition that is far worse. That is when people say all evil against us truly. Many accusations against us carry a certain percentage of truth in them. It is this portion that the Lord would have us to reckon with, rather than decrying the overstatement. While these falsities levied against us may raise our ire, they are not the reason we stumble and walk around with consequential bruises. Offense arises when the opinion of another doesn't measure up to the extent we tout ourselves.

“Cast ye up, cast ye up, prepare the way, take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people. For thus saith the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy; I dwell in the high and holy place, with him also that is of a contrite and humble spirit, to revive the spirit of the humble, and to revive the heart of the contrite ones” (Isaiah 57:14-15). Here, Isaiah instructs us to remove the stumbling block but makes no mention of the offender. The antidote is to be of a contrite and humble spirit. We will never be able to exterminate every avenue of offense. But if reckoned correctly, there is no offense that shall ever be able to divert us from the promise, “they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint” (Isaiah 40:31). It is predominantly our pride which stands in the way of our successful journey, rather than ill-treatment.

Walk In Love

“And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet smelling savour. But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting . . .” (Ephesians 5:2-4). It takes no scholar to observe the stumblings of a selfish fool. This selfish ambition to obtain friends, wealth, and affluence is guaranteed to bring a man flat on his nose at some time or another. The trail of sins mentioned here are all following in tow to the gratifying of self. King Ahasuerus counseled of Haman on how to honor a worthy man. Haman’s narcissistic mind immediately brooded, “To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?” (Esther 6:6). God had other plans thus the man who was so offended by Mordecai was hung upon the gallows of his own creation. Selfish souls can point to a thousand and one reasons why they are not attaining their aspirations. Somebody wronged them. An unfortunate turn of events derailed them. But it was not Mordecai, Esther, nor even Ahasuerus that brought Haman stumbling to his bitter end. It was his own refusal to walk in love and to sacrifice himself for others that wrought the malignant demise in his soul.

Walk as Children of Light

“Walk as children of light . . . proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them” (Ephesians 5:8-11). Our innate passions contain the third rock of offense. There may be things that we believe are acceptable to our Lord, which are not. There are those who have “itching ears; and they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables” (2 Timothy 4:3-4). This may affect those with the most noble intentions and firm beliefs. Christ forewarned His disciples that they would be put out of the synagogues so that when it happened, they “should not be offended” (John 16:1-4).

John the Baptist was a burning and a shining light and no prophet born of women had risen greater. He walked worthy of his calling, baptized the Lord, and rebuked the Pharisees. He walked in love, and multitudes “were willing for a season to rejoice in his light” (John 5:35). Yet the day came when he sent his disciples to ask Jesus: Art thou he that should come? Or look we for another? To which Jesus replied, “Go your way, and tell John what things ye have seen and heard; how that the blind see, the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed, the deaf hear, the dead are raised, to the poor the gospel is preached ... and blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me” (Luke 7:20-23). Christ's response would indicate that this apparently did not fully fit the aspirations of what John had in mind, and he was struggling to accept it. Like his Old Testament counterpart, Elijah, these like passions provided the fodder for the flames of discouragement. It seemed to John that evil had enveloped the nation and God wasn't doing His part.

We may mean well, but our own passionate feelings are not a good gauge of proving what is acceptable unto the Lord. Phaltiel was a dear soul who fell into such deceit. He had been given Michal by King Saul himself. The princess was no doubt a delicate and pleasing prize. David had evidently valued her so, for he risked his life and doubled the dowry with two hundred Philistine foreskins to secure her hand in marriage. But Phaltiel thought nothing of that, relishing his own good fortune and so enjoyed her company for years. Though this arrangement may have been socially acceptable at the time, no man has the right to receive what another has no right to give. The day came when “they sent, and took her from her husband, even from Phaltiel the son of Laish. And her husband went with her along weeping behind her” (2 Samuel 3:15-16). We know very little of Phaltiel, but if we dismiss ourselves from his emotional avalanche, we must declare him faulty. We dare not let our compassionate heart turn toward him or toward anyone who is offended when asked to separate from works of darkness. When these passionate feelings are allowed to rule, offense is the inevitable result. “For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? But if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God” (1 Peter 2:20) . . .

Walk Circumspectly

“See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise” (Ephesians 5:15). “Be not children in understanding: howbeit in malice be ye children, but in understanding be men” (1 Corinthians 14:20). Herein we must honestly acknowledge that ignorance is not bliss. To enter the narrow gate may require a broad mind. Not so broad to allow sin, but broad enough to allow God. Circumspect is a compound word formed from the Latin words circum (around) and spectare (to behold). The one-dimensional soul will spend his days being offended, for he cannot see from the viewpoint of any but his own. There are over a dozen solid scriptures warning us against doing what is right in our own eyes. We must learn to honestly consider the counsel and wisdom of others lest we fall into condemnation.

In her early years, Michal loved David with deep and fervent loyalty but later fell prey to rash judgment. “As the ark of the LORD came into the city of David, Michal, Saul's daughter looked through a window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before the LORD; and she despised him in her heart” (2 Samuel 6:16). As Michal viewed the scene from her upper vantage, there were two things evident. First, David was exuberantly thankful, and his joy knew no bounds. This is first love, “for whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God” (2 Corinthians 5:13). Second, during David's ecstatic dancing in his loin cloth, his discretion elapsed, and his flesh became a bit public. This would require great circumspection to view from another portal, and Michal will have none of it. Upon his entrance to bless his house, David was met with a blast of pent-up bigotry from his offended and sarcastic wife. While the accusation carried a dimension of truth, to cling to it as supreme was shameful prejudice. God had no sympathy for it and “therefore Michal the daughter of Saul had no child unto the day of her death” (2 Samuel 6:23). Many a good woman has judged her man from her singular corner and parched the soil of the home with the same arid judgment. This narrow-mindedness will never be fruitful no matter how blatant the accusation. There is a correct way to express concern, but the outpouring of biased judgment will turn a celestial oasis into a barren wasteland in a prompt fashion.

“A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city: and their contentions are like the bars of a castle” (Proverbs 18:19). So it is with a sister, husband, wife, friend, etc. While causes for offense abound on every side, does Christ desire us to be offended? Will He salute our sour and shriveled soul? Perhaps He gave us this test so that we may have root within ourselves, “that no man should be moved by these afflictions” (1 Thessalonians 3:3). While we may not be able to control our feelings during times of inward pain, we each can choose a redemptive path and walk in the Spirit. It is a choice to broadcast grievances, nurse hurts, withdraw from the offender, and decline to believe all things. Like the brother offended, these contentions serve to lock the soul like the bars of a castle. But who holds the power for release?

J doute qu'il existe une âme vivante qui n'ait été offensée à un moment ou à un autre. Les mauvaises herbes persistantes de l'influence du mal semblent pousser à chaque coin, mettant à l'épreuve les meilleures relations en fleur. Plus nous possédons d'outils de communication, plus nous semblons rencontrer de malentendus, et les gens sont offensés. Aujourd'hui, on attend des ministres de l'Évangile qu'ils soient doux et efféminés de peur d'offenser leurs auditeurs. Bien que nous devions certainement rencontrer les gens là où ils sont et chercher à ne pas les offenser, le fléau de l'église moderne n'est pas le ministre hardi et offensant.

Je ne veux donner aucune licence aux prédicateurs endurcis qui sont dépourvus de tendresse et de larmes. Malheur aux prophètes aux yeux secs qui brandissent l'épée du Seigneur sans la moindre considération pour les personnes réelles entre lesquelles ils coupent dans le processus. Pourtant, il semble qu'il y ait une épidémie de notre époque qui a surpassé la peste bubonique, dépassé les ravages de la polio, et fait paraître notre cancer moderne comme une simple gêne. Je parle de l'éclosion des millions de cœurs offensés qui surgissent des décombres des innombrables hordes de relations brisées et tendues autour de nous en toute direction. Jésus a mentionné que l'un des signes des derniers temps est que « alors plusieurs seront scandalisés... et ils se haïront les uns les autres » (Matthieu 24:10). Les foyers frappés par le divorce ont atteint un niveau record, produisant une génération de méfiance et de douleur immenses. Les couples se jugeront incompatibles et se sépareront à la moindre offense. Des chrétiens passeront des années en dehors d'un cadre d'église parce qu'ils ont été offensés par des frères en Christ.

Beaucoup prendront automatiquement le parti de la personne offensée, la supposant victime. Bien souvent, ils le sont. « Malheur au monde à cause des scandales ! » (Matthieu 18:7) Mais l'équation change quand nous considérons que le Christ sans péché a offensé beaucoup de gens. Il dit à ses disciples qu'ils devaient manger sa chair et beaucoup le quittèrent. Il informa les douze intimes qui étaient restés avec lui : « Vous tous serez scandalisés à mon sujet cette nuit » (Marc 14:27). Les pharisiens furent offensés lorsque le Christ exposa leur culte vain, et Jésus offensa même ses compatriotes simplement en faisant le bien. Le mot grec est skandalízō signifiant « scandaliser ».1 En hébreu, il signifie « une pierre d'achoppement ». Le problème est que beaucoup aujourd'hui trébuchent à la moindre obstruction sur leur chemin et que la taupinière devient une montagne.

« Une grande paix ont ceux qui aiment ta loi : et rien ne les scandalise » (Psaume 119:165). Que devons-nous dire alors de ce passage ? Ici sont des gens qui ont appris à marcher sur le chemin rocailleux de la vie sans tomber à chaque fois qu'un obstacle déplaisant se présente devant eux. Nous ne voulons pas condamner l'âme sensible, mais le mot « sensible » n'est pas dans la Bible. Le mot le plus proche que nous y trouvons est sensuel, qui est très similaire dans ses racines et signifie naturel. Le Christ décrivit ces plantes comme n'ayant « pas de racine en eux, mais ils durent un moment : et quand la tribulation ou la persécution survient à cause de la parole, aussitôt il est scandalisé » (Matthieu 13:20-21). Il est si facile et très naturel d'avoir pitié des offensés. Ils portent une histoire déchirante, et ils la partagent généralement en larmes. « En beaucoup de choses nous péchons tous » (Jacques 3:2). Personne n'est aussi irréprochable dans son offense que le Christ, si bien qu'il y a généralement un élément de vérité déversé contre l'offenseur. Il me semble que nous serions tous beaucoup plus loin si nous retenions une partie de notre sympathie pour les offensés et consacrions nos énergies à leur apprendre comment marcher droit sur le chemin de la vie malgré les pierres d'achoppement aiguës et copieuses qui nous accueillent chaque jour sur notre parcours. Nous apprendrons à vivre sans être offensés quand nous apprendrons à...

Marcher dignement

« Je vous exhorte donc, moi, le prisonnier dans le Seigneur, à marcher d'une manière digne de la vocation dont vous avez été appelés, avec toute humilité et douceur, avec patience, vous supportant les uns les autres avec amour » (Éphésiens 4:1-2). Marcher dignement, comme Paul le décrit ici, c'est marcher dans l'humilité. « L'orgueil va devant la ruine, et l'esprit hautain devant la chute » (Proverbes 16:18). Plus notre vaisseau est chargé d'orgueil, plus nous sommes sujets à être offensés. Plus nous évaluons honnêtement notre valeur, moins nous serons offensés quand on nous ridiculise. Plus d'humilité égale moins d'achoppement. Lorsqu'on nous accuse à tort, cela fait toujours mal. Jésus dit que nous devrions être heureux quand on dira toutes sortes de mal de nous faussement. Bien qu'une telle blessure dégradante puisse suppurer sous notre peau, il existe une condition bien pire : c'est quand les gens disent tout le mal véritablement contre nous. Beaucoup d'accusations portées contre nous contiennent un certain pourcentage de vérité. C'est cette portion que le Seigneur voudrait que nous prenions en compte, plutôt que de dénoncer l'exagération. Ces faussetés lancées contre nous peuvent éveiller notre colère, mais elles ne sont pas la raison pour laquelle nous trébuchons et portons des contusions conséquentes. L'offense naît quand l'opinion d'un autre ne correspond pas à l'exagération que nous faisons de nous-mêmes.

« Rebâtissez, rebâtissez, préparez le chemin, ôtez les pierres d'achoppement du chemin de mon peuple. Car ainsi parle celui qui est très haut et qui habite l'éternité, dont le nom est Saint : j'habite en un lieu élevé et saint, et aussi avec celui qui est contrit et humilié d'esprit, pour ranimer l'esprit des humbles, et pour ranimer le cœur des contrits » (Isaïe 57:14-15). Ici, Isaïe nous instruit d'enlever la pierre d'achoppement mais ne mentionne pas l'offenseur. L'antidote est d'avoir un esprit contrit et humble. Nous ne pourrons jamais exterminer toutes les sources d'offense. Mais si nous y prenons garde correctement, il n'y a aucune offense qui pourra jamais nous détourner de la promesse : « ils monteront avec des ailes comme des aigles; ils courront, et ne se fatigueront point; ils marcheront, et ne se lasseront point » (Isaïe 40:31). C'est principalement notre orgueil qui fait obstacle à notre voyage réussi, plutôt que le mauvais traitement.

Marcher dans l'amour

« Marchez dans l'amour, comme Christ aussi nous a aimés, et s'est livré lui-même pour nous en offrande et en sacrifice à Dieu, en parfum agréable. Mais la fornication, et toute impureté, ou la cupidité, qu'on n'en parle même pas parmi vous, comme il convient à des saints; ni d'impudicité, ni de propos insensés, ni de plaisanteries... » (Éphésiens 5:2-4). Il ne faut pas être savant pour observer les chutes d'un fou égoïste. Cette ambition égoïste d'obtenir des amis, des richesses et de l'aisance garantit qu'un homme finira par tomber à plat nez à un moment ou à un autre. La traînée de péchés mentionnée ici suit tous le chemin vers la satisfaction de soi. Le roi Assuérus conseilla à Haman comment honorer un homme digne. L'esprit narcissique d'Haman pensa aussitôt : « À qui le roi plairait-il de faire davantage honneur que moi ? » (Esther 6:6). Dieu avait d'autres desseins ; ainsi l'homme qui était si offensé par Mardochée fut pendu au gibet de sa propre création. Les âmes égoïstes peuvent avancer mille et une raisons pour lesquelles elles n'atteignent pas leurs aspirations. Quelqu'un les a lésées. Un malheureux enchaînement d'événements les a déraillées. Mais ce n'était ni Mardochée, ni Esther, ni même Assuérus qui firent tomber Haman jusqu'à sa fin amère. Ce fut son propre refus de marcher dans l'amour et de se sacrifier pour les autres qui causa la maligne perte de son âme.

Marcher comme des enfants de lumière

« Marchez comme des enfants de lumière... éprouvant ce qui est agréable au Seigneur. Et n'ayez point de communion avec les œuvres infructueuses des ténèbres, mais plutôt reprenez-les » (Éphésiens 5:8-11). Nos passions innées contiennent la troisième pierre d'offense. Il peut y avoir des choses que nous croyons agréables à notre Seigneur, et qui ne le sont pas. Il y a ceux qui ont « des oreilles qui démangent; et ils détourneront leurs oreilles de la vérité, et se tourneront vers des fables » (2 Timothée 4:3-4). Cela peut affecter ceux qui ont les intentions les plus nobles et des convictions fermes. Le Christ prévint ses disciples qu'ils seraient chassés des synagogues afin que, lorsque cela arriverait, ils « ne soient pas scandalisés » (Jean 16:1-4).

Jean-Baptiste était une lumière ardente et resplendissante et aucun prophète né de femme ne s'est levé plus grand. Il marcha dignement de son appel, baptisa le Seigneur, et réprimanda les pharisiens. Il marcha dans l'amour, et les foules « se plaisaient pour un temps à se réjouir dans sa lumière » (Jean 5:35). Pourtant le jour vint où il envoya ses disciples demander à Jésus : « Es-tu celui qui doit venir ? Ou devons-nous en attendre un autre ? » Jésus répondit : « Allez, rapportez à Jean ce que vous avez vu et entendu; comment les aveugles voient, les boiteux marchent, les lépreux sont purifiés, les sourds entendent, les morts ressuscitent, et la bonne nouvelle est annoncée aux pauvres... et heureux est celui qui ne sera pas scandalisé en moi » (Luc 7:20-23). La réponse du Christ indiquerait que cela ne correspondait apparemment pas entièrement aux aspirations que Jean avait en tête, et il avait du mal à l'accepter. Comme son homologue de l'Ancien Testament, Élie, ces mêmes passions fournissaient le combustible aux flammes du découragement. Il semblait à Jean que le mal avait enveloppé la nation et que Dieu ne faisait pas sa part.

Nous pouvons avoir de bonnes intentions, mais nos propres sentiments passionnés ne sont pas un bon étalon pour éprouver ce qui est agréable au Seigneur. Paltiel fut une âme chère qui tomba dans une telle tromperie. Il avait reçu Michal du roi Saül lui-même. La princesse était sans doute un prix délicat et séduisant. David l'avait manifestement tant estimée qu'il risqua sa vie et doubla la dot avec deux cents prépuces philistins pour obtenir sa main en mariage. Mais Paltiel n'en tint pas compte, savourant sa bonne fortune et profitant de sa compagnie pendant des années. Bien que cette situation ait pu être socialement acceptable à l'époque, nul homme n'a le droit de recevoir ce qu'un autre n'a pas le droit de donner. Le jour vint où « ils l'envoyèrent et la prirent de son mari, même de Paltiel, fils de Laïsh. Et son mari l'accompagna en pleurant derrière elle » (2 Samuel 3:15-16). Nous savons très peu de Paltiel, mais si nous nous excluons de son avalanche émotionnelle, nous devons le déclarer fautif. Nous n'osons pas laisser notre cœur compatissant se tourner vers lui ou vers quiconque est offensé quand on lui demande de se séparer des œuvres des ténèbres. Quand ces sentiments passionnés sont laissés dominer, l'offense est le résultat inévitable. « Car quel est l'avantage, si, lorsque vous frappez pour vos fautes, vous le supportez patiemment ? Mais si, lorsque vous faites bien et que vous souffrez pour cela, vous le supportez patiemment, ceci est agréable devant Dieu » (1 Pierre 2:20) ...

Marcher avec circonspection

« Prenez donc garde à votre marche, que ce ne soit pas comme des insensés, mais comme des sages » (Éphésiens 5:15). « Ne soyez pas enfants dans l'entendement : soyez, au contraire, des hommes dans l'entendement; et dans la malice, soyez des enfants » (1 Corinthiens 14:20). Ici, nous devons reconnaître honnêtement que l'ignorance n'est pas une béatitude. Entrer par la porte étroite peut nécessiter un esprit large. Pas assez large pour permettre le péché, mais assez large pour permettre à Dieu. Circonspect est un mot composé formé des mots latins circum (autour) et spectare (regarder). L'âme unidimensionnelle passera ses jours à être offensée, car elle ne peut voir que son propre point de vue. Il y a plus d'une douzaine de solides Écritures qui nous avertissent contre le fait de faire ce qui est juste à nos propres yeux. Nous devons apprendre à considérer honnêtement les conseils et la sagesse des autres de peur de tomber dans la condamnation.

Dans ses premières années, Michal aimait profondément et ardemment David mais tomba plus tard victime d'un jugement irréfléchi. « Comme l'arche du SEIGNEUR entrait dans la ville de David, Michal, fille de Saül, regarda par une fenêtre, et vit le roi David sautant et dansant devant le SEIGNEUR; et elle le méprisa en son cœur » (2 Samuel 6:16). Tandis que Michal observait la scène depuis sa haute loge, deux choses étaient évidentes. Premièrement, David exprimait une reconnaissance exubérante, et sa joie ne connaissait pas de bornes. C'est le premier amour, « car si nous sommes déraisonnables, c'est pour Dieu » (2 Corinthiens 5:13). Deuxièmement, pendant la danse extatique de David dans son linge de corps, sa discrétion fit défaut, et sa chair devint un peu publique. Cela aurait requis une grande circonspection pour le voir depuis un autre point de vue, et Michal n'en voulut rien savoir. À son entrée pour bénir sa maison, David fut accueilli par un flot de bigoterie refoulée de la part de sa femme offensée et sarcastique. Bien que l'accusation portât une dimension de vérité, s'y attacher comme s'il s'agissait de la suprême réalité était un honteux préjugé. Dieu n'eut aucune sympathie pour cela et « ainsi Michal, la fille de Saül, n'eut point d'enfant jusqu'au jour de sa mort » (2 Samuel 6:23). Beaucoup de bonnes femmes ont jugé leur homme depuis leur coin singulier et asséché le sol du foyer par ce même jugement aride. Cet étroitesse d'esprit ne portera jamais de fruit, si flagrante que soit l'accusation. Il y a une manière correcte d'exprimer une inquiétude, mais le déversement d'un jugement partial transformera promptement une oasis céleste en un désert stérile.

« Un frère offensé est plus difficile à gagner qu'une ville forte: et leurs dissensions sont comme les barres d'une forteresse » (Proverbes 18:19). Bien que nous ne puissions pas toujours contrôler nos sentiments en des temps de douleur intérieure, nous pouvons chacun choisir une voie rédemptrice et marcher dans l'Esprit. C'est un choix que de diffuser ses griefs, de soigner ses blessures, de se retirer de l'offenseur, et de refuser de croire toutes choses. Comme le frère offensé, ces dissensions servent à verrouiller l'âme comme les barres d'une forteresse. Mais qui détient le pouvoir de la délivrance ?

The message was brief. “Dr. Waldron, would you call Mrs. Jones back about her labs?”

I was puzzled. I didn’t remember ordering any labs for Mrs. Jones. As far as I could remember, she was seeing a specialist and just had surgery for colon cancer. Maybe they had ordered the labs. But if so, they certainly should have followed up on them.

I opened the chart and looked in the lab section. Quickly my eye went to my patient’s kidney function and stopped. Her kidney function had declined a huge amount in the last week.

I called her and then her kidney specialist. Over the next half hour, her situation came into view. Because of her colon surgery, she was losing a lot of fluid, enough that she couldn’t keep up. This, in turn, was making her kidney function a lot worse, along with dropping her potassium level.

To take care of it, she would need IV fluids – once or twice a week – to keep up with the fluids she was losing. Without that, her kidneys would shut down completely.

In a sense, Mrs. Jones was dealing with kidney burnout—a situation where they were putting out more than they were taking in and suffering as a result.

As I was thinking about this, my mind went to the Dead Sea. The Dead Sea is “Dead” because it has such a high level of minerals and salts that very few, other than a few microorganisms, can survive.

The reason for this is that the Dead Sea has no outlet. The Jordan River drains into it, carrying fresh water, and then sits in a basin. Some of the water evaporates, and what remains are the salts and minerals in the water.

Over the thousands of years since the fall of Sodom and Gomorrah, this inland body of water has become one of the saltiest places on earth. It is a body of water that is neither useful for irrigation nor a place where plants and animals can thrive.

Neither situation is healthy, yet this is exactly how most people live their lives, typically gravitating towards one pole or the other. Either they fill their schedule to the maximum, leaving no time for quiet reflection, or they resist any efforts to get them to invest their time and talents and avoid these sorts of activities.

I want to spend a little time thinking about burnout. What causes it, and how we can avoid it?

Everyone has Limits

I Samuel 30 tells the story of David returning to Ziklag. Upon his arrival, he discovered, to his dismay, that the Amalekites had invaded Philistine territory, burned the town, and taken captive all the people who were present.

David and his men had been gone three days and were already tired from their journey to and from Aphek, where King Agag had mustered his forces. Despite this and their anguish at the loss of their family members and material possessions, David consulted God and decided to pursue to the Amalekites out into the desert.

They had only gone as far as the Brook Besor when a third of his men gave up. Scripture tells us they were “too faint” to cross the brook. They were physically and mentally exhausted. Even if they had been able to hold things together for another day, they would be useless in battle.

So it was that David left them behind and continued to pursue the Amalekites, eventually defeating them with the four hundred men who were able to persevere. Here, we come to the interesting part. The men who had won the victory looked down on the men who had been faint. They said those faint-hearted men could have their families back, but all the spoil would be reserved for those who had won the victory.

In response, David said, “Ye shall not do so, my brethren, with that which the Lord hath given us, who hath preserved us, and delivered the company that came against us into our hand. For who will hearken unto you in this matter? but as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff: they shall part alike.” (I Samuel 30:23,24)

David did not wish to penalize those who had tried but did not have the strength to make it through to the final battle.

Perhaps this speaks of the grace we ought to extend to others who don’t have the strength or energy to continue for a season. Maybe it lets us know that we should extend that same grace to ourselves.

What is Burnout?

There are different definitions for burnout, but it all comes down to a state of physical, mental, or emotional exhaustion related to too much stress over an extended period of time. We tend to think of this stress as work-related. There are too many projects going on at once, not enough help, or an employer who has high expectations.

Stress is stress, and it all adds up. Even if work isn’t stressful, if you have a newborn baby at home, a family member with dementia, or many church responsibilities, you can still reach the place where you have little left to give.

It is as though you are in a vehicle traveling 90 mph, and you push the accelerator a little harder, and nothing happens. In response, you push the gas pedal even harder, and a screeching noise comes from the engine. Suddenly, the dashboard lights up with funny lights, and the car starts to slow down.

The question is, how can we avoid burnout and what should we do if we realize that we are heading towards it?

Understanding Burnout

Burnout leads to both physical and emotional depletion. The problem with burnout is that even if a particular stressor causes it – say, a situation at work or a family health problem – it will affect numerous other relationships.

People dealing with burnout often exhibit symptoms consistent with depression and anxiety. They may become withdrawn, lack motivation to be involved with church and family activities, or get angry quicker than people who are not dealing with burnout.

There is even a suggestion that burnout can lead to the weakening of our immune systems. This could lead to more colds and viral infections.

Identify Early Signs

We need to know ourselves. There are signs that other people can see in our lives and how we relate to others that we don’t necessarily identify as a problem.

People who are on the edge of burnout feel hopeless. They may hide it from their coworkers, but often, their family members realize that something is wrong. You used to have a sunny disposition, and now you are discouraged, not only about the present but also the future.

You might lack motivation and have low energy levels. In a sense, you are going through the motions and just doing enough to get by – both at work and in your home. This is likely related to your feelings of hopelessness.

You may find that you are more irritable than you used to be. Little things bother or aggravate you, and you find yourself smothering angry retorts.

It is important to realize that you are heading down this road for several reasons. First, you are not the only one who suffers when you are burned out. Your family must deal with you and your “grumpiness.” Also, the longer you go without taking care of things, the harder it is to get back to a place of balance.

As a physician, I see people all the time who “didn’t have time” to get something taken care of until they could no longer ignore it. At this point, it will take a major procedure to set things right. It would have been easier to correct if they came in with the first symptom.

Make a Priority List

Everything in our life has a priority level. People who do not prioritize end up feeling scattered as they try to do everything at once. This is a recipe for disaster. To me, it makes sense to divide our tasks into four buckets:

  1. Things that need to be done relatively quickly
  2. Things that need to be done but can wait a bit
  3. Things that we’d like to do, but don’t need to
  4. Things that we should let go of.

Here might be a good place to mention that just because something needs to be done does not mean you need to do it. Sometimes, someone in your home or workplace could help with one of the tasks on your to-do list.

Once we have made our priority list, we need to do something about it. If you simply assign a priority to everything in your life but continue to try to do everything, it won’t help your situation at all.

The point of this exercise is to figure out what things you can eliminate from your schedule, so you have more space to breathe.

Make First Things First

One of the things that happens when we are overwhelmed is that we stop doing self-care. We grab unhealthy food on the go, stop spending time in prayer and devotions, and quit exercising.

Doing these things takes time, and that is exactly what we think we don’t have when we are living on the margins of our energy. Self-care is extremely important but often gets assigned a priority of zero and is seldom included in a day’s activity.

As we begin to replenish our spiritual nourishment, we must also make sure we take care of our physical health.

Take Time Apart

After feeding the multitudes, Mark 6:46 tells of Jesus, “And when he had sent them away, he departed into a mountain to pray.” Even Jesus had times when He needed to be alone without distractions.

It is easy to focus on the prayer aspect of this passage, and that is important, but let's focus on the solitary aspect of this experience. Jesus even left His closest followers behind during this time of seeking God’s face.

There are times when we need to escape from the pressure of human interactions and find a peaceful place where we can be alone.

Put Down Technology

Part of making rest time truly restful is to eliminate sources of distraction. Phones and electronic tablets are exactly the types of things that can keep our minds from achieving the peace (shalom) that we both desire and need.

Digital burnout is a new term that is being used to describe people who feel apathetic and exhausted from spending hours each day staring at screens. Many workers spend seven or eight hours a day looking at computer screens and then get even more screen time after work.

The funny thing is that the most productive workers are often people who use old-fashioned things like paper calendars and leave phones out of meetings. As wonderful as phones are, they are also immensely distracting for most of us.

So often, we have time away that is simply not restful. The reason is that we continue to receive texts and emails and can still access social media. If you are not someone who can put his phone away and ignore it (it takes a lot of willpower to do this), then leave your phone in another room and create some distance. This will seem stressful, but we can focus on recharging ourselves by creating a screen-free zone.

Build Breaks into Your Day

There is a certain amount of work that must be done each day, and it often feels like too much for the allotted 24 hours. There is certainly no time to stop, stretch, and take a five-minute walk, or at least that's what we tell ourselves.

In reality, if you take a five-minute break every few hours to do something non-work related, you will come back refreshed and more ready to deal with the problems of the day.

Do something healthy during this time. Take a short walk or eat an apple. Chowing down a bag of potato chips or eating a couple candy bars is not likely to produce the desired results.

The problem is often with our own expectations. People who struggle with burnout often have extremely high personal standards and get frustrated when they not measure up to that standard.

Be Intentional about Rest

One of the messages of the Old Testament was the importance of the Sabbath. I have heard many people argue that in the New Testament period, we no longer need to practice the Sabbath. Didn’t Paul say that one day was like the other? Didn’t Jesus defend His disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath?

Regardless of what you believe about the importance of keeping the Sabbath, it is still important that we take time to rest. This is the real message that Jesus was conveying when He said that the “Sabbath was created for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Rest is not simply sleeping till 10 am and then doing nothing. Rest is actively making decisions that will help us recharge our depleted batteries. Go out for breakfast with a friend, take a hike, or take a good book and go somewhere without cell service and focus on something other than situations that are depleting you.

Jesus understood the human need for rest, this is why He told His disciples “Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while” (Mark 6:31). This time of rest would give them energy for their next time of ministry.

Don’t Buy into Myths

People tell themselves all sorts of lies that can lead to pushing themselves too hard. I’ll list a few of them and some thoughts about each one.

“I’m the only one who can do this task.” This feels true. The other people in our home or workplace are not helping us the way we wish that they would. Sometimes, it simply feels easier to do the task ourselves rather than spend time teaching someone else how to do it. We need to remember that if we died, the people around us would figure out how to get things done. We can assign them some of the tasks today before we die.

“If I just get this job done today, tomorrow will be easier.” I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but each day has 24 hours, and somehow, they always get filled up. I have given up the idea that there is a time in my life coming up soon that will have nothing on the schedule. If a rest comes, it will come because I have made an effort to clear my schedule, not because by some random occurrence, one day, I happen to not have a single task in it.

“God will never give me more than I can handle.” God has promised many things. He has promised that when there is a temptation, He will give us an opportunity to escape it (I Corinthians 10:13). He has also promised that He will never leave us or forsake us (Hebrews 13:5). I do not read anywhere in Scripture that God will keep us from overfilling our lives. He has simply promised that He will give us opportunity to take a different path and will walk beside us on our way.

So often the heavy load we carry is because other people, or even we, ourselves, have put too many things on our task list. Suppose I choose to put too many patients on my schedule and I am feeling exhausted. In that case, it is time for me to take responsibility for what I have done, rather than claiming a mythical promise that God will keep me from overwhelming myself.

“These are all good things that I am doing.” Doctors face this a lot. We want to squeeze one more patient into the schedule and stay just a little later to answer another message because we feel responsible. We hate to think that someone might need to go to the Emergency Department because we did not take care of them when they needed help.

Just because the things in your schedule are “good things” that benefit other people and are building the kingdom, does not mean that you don’t need to cut back in one area or another. If you are feeling emotionally depleted, it is probably time to remove a few items from your to-do list.

Conclusion

There are other things that could be mentioned. Getting support from someone else, meditating on Scripture, and even taking a vacation are all things that can help.

When I read about some of the famous preachers of the past, I see in some of their lives a roller coaster. They pushed themselves to the max, got involved in large numbers of projects, and then had an emotional breakdown. They would take some time off and, a month or two later, launch back into the same activities. This cycle continued for their whole ministry.

Jesus tells us that His yoke is easy, and His burden is light (Matt, 11:28-30). If we are at the point of exhaustion, we need to consider whether we have Jesus’ yoke or if we are laboring under the burden of our own creation.

Jesus knows our limitations. He wants us to have balance, living in such a way that we not only have strength for today but also for tomorrow, next week, and next year – till He comes again.
